display.title: What's Your Wish? The Power of Joy
display.summary_short: Why we daven, told through a king's open invitation; the storyteller's own childhood lesson about davening properly; and a Chassid whose Simchas Torah dancing saves his son.
display.summary_long: After the song "I believe in Hashem", the storyteller gives a mashal: a king lets every citizen ask for one wish, and one wise man asks for a pass to visit the king every day. Hashem gives us that pass three times a day, so we should speak to Him clearly and with respect. He then shares something from his own childhood: as a young boy he found the siddur too long, so he only turned pages and moved his lips. He later learned the Shulchan Aruch's rule that a little with kavanah is better than a lot without it, and a Rav told him children may begin with the main parts, such as Shema and Shemoneh Esreh, as a first step and add more over time. For the coming summer, he urges children to really daven. The story: a Chassid of the Tzemach Tzedek travels to Lubavitch for a brachah for his gravely ill son and receives only a vague answer. He weeps over Tehillim until the hakafos of Shemini Atzeres, then realizes Hashem wants him to dance, and dances with all his strength through Simchas Torah. The Tzemach Tzedek tells him his joy broke a harsh decree, and he finds his son healthy.
display.lesson: Daven every day with clear words, even if you start with only the main parts, and serve Hashem with simcha, which brings every brachah.

advisories.note: A boy is gravely ill and doctors say he may not live; he recovers completely.
